title: Connect to a Registered Nurse 24/7 with the Global Nurse Advice Line
description:
What is the Global Nurse Advice Line?
The Global Nurse Advice Line, or GNAL, connects eligible beneficiaries worldwide with registered nurses who can assess symptoms, provide evidence-based health advice and recommend the appropriate level of care.
What services can the advice line provide?
The advice line can also help patients understand how to seek care when they have other health insurance.
For military health care providers, the advice line can help assess incoming patients and direct them to the appropriate level of care.
text:
By Rodney Jackson, Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center Public Affairs

FORT HOOD, Texas – Fort Hood-area service members, retirees and their families enrolled in TRICARE can get health advice and help finding appropriate care through the Global Nurse Advice Line, available 24/7 and 365 days a year.

What is the Global Nurse Advice Line?

The Global Nurse Advice Line, or GNAL, connects eligible beneficiaries worldwide with registered nurses who can assess symptoms, provide evidence-based health advice and recommend the appropriate level of care. A quick call or online chat may help patients determine whether they need urgent care, an emergency room or an appointment with their primary care provider.

The service also assists with scheduling same-day or next-day appointments when a nurse recommends one. This appointment assistance is available to beneficiaries enrolled at a military hospital or clinic. Virtual urgent care may also be available in some cases.

How can beneficiaries contact the advice line?

Beneficiaries in the United States, Guam and Puerto Rico can access the service by visiting the MHS Nurse Advice Line at https://mhsnurseadviceline.com/home for web chat or video chat, or by calling 800-TRICARE (874-2273) and selecting option 1.

Before contacting GNAL, beneficiaries should have their Department of Defense benefit number available. The number can be found on their military ID card.

Is the service available to beneficiaries stationed or traveling overseas?

Yes. The service is available to eligible TRICARE beneficiaries worldwide, including those stationed or traveling overseas.

Beneficiaries near an overseas military hospital or clinic can contact their local facility or visit the MHS Nurse Advice Line at https://mhsnurseadviceline.com/home to access online services and country-specific telephone numbers. When care is needed outside the Military Health System, GNAL can coordinate with the TRICARE overseas contractor.

What services can the advice line provide?

In addition to assessing symptoms, nurses can provide guidance for parents whose children are sick, help beneficiaries determine where to seek care and, when medically appropriate, provide an online absence excuse or sick slip. Beneficiaries should check their service-specific requirements for accepting such documentation.

The advice line can also help patients understand how to seek care when they have other health insurance. However, the rules of the other health insurance plan apply first, and any referred provider must be within that plan’s network.

Who is eligible to use the service?

The service is available to TRICARE beneficiaries worldwide, with exceptions for those enrolled in the US Family Health Plan or TRICARE Prime Demo, which have their own nurse advice lines.

Beneficiaries should keep their information current in the Defense Enrollment Eligibility Reporting System, or DEERS, through milConnect to help ensure their eligibility.

How does GNAL support military health care providers?

For military health care providers, the advice line can help assess incoming patients and direct them to the appropriate level of care. This support can help organize appointment scheduling and guide patients to the services best suited to their needs.

What should beneficiaries do in an emergency?

GNAL is intended for health advice and care navigation, not emergencies. Anyone experiencing a medical emergency should call 911 in the United States or the applicable international emergency number overseas, or go to the nearest emergency room.

text:
FORT DRUM, N.Y. (Nov. 4, 2026) -- Fort Drum community members gathered inside The Peak ballroom Nov. 4 for the monthly Community Information Exchange to learn about upcoming seasonal events, winter readiness programs, gate schedule changes and support resources.

Brig. Gen. Joseph Ewers, 10th Mountain Division (LI) and Fort Drum commanding general, said he was pleased to see company-level leaders and spouses in attendance, and asked them to relay the information to their formations and their families.

“This Community Information Exchange is a resource that ultimately informs and prepares those leaders who are going to be doing that final engagement – that final hundred yards, as they say – with our families,” he said. “We owe it to them to set the conditions for their self-reliance; that we don’t just point at them and say, ‘Be self-reliant. Be resilient.’ What are we doing to enable that resiliency? It starts with information.”

Ewers said that a key component to a great unit is having informed families, which is something he aspires to continue within the 10th Mountain Division (LI).

“Informed families start here,” he said. “We are here as their representatives. This is where the information begins. It ends at the families.”

Holiday Gate Closures

The Directorate of Emergency Services provided updates on installation access and community safety. Due to ongoing construction, the Gas Alley access control point remains closed.

The Lt. Gen. Paul Cerjan access control point and the Wheeler-Sack Army Airfield access control point continue 24/7 operations.

The Plummer Gate will observe the following holiday closure schedule:

Thanksgiving Weekend: Closes at 10 p.m. Nov. 25, and reopens at 4:30 a.m. Nov. 30.

Christmas / New Year Block Leave: Closes at 10 p.m. Dec. 19 and reopens at 5:30 a.m. Jan. 3.

Fort Drum DES is partnering with the New York State Police to host a free Child Safety Seat Installation and Inspection event starting at 10 a.m. on Nov. 21, at Fire Station 2, Bldg. 1585 on Ontario Avenue. Drivers can pull directly through the fire station bay doors in a dedicated inspection lane to have car seats inspected or properly installed.

With peak holiday shipping underway, DES advised residents to protect deliveries from porch theft by:

Using secure drop-off lockers, counters, or local carrier pickup sites (such as UPS or FedEx Office locations).

Enabling delivery alerts and text notifications to retrieve packages immediately upon drop-off.

Placing carrier holds or scheduling deliveries for times when someone is home; avoiding leaving boxes unattended overnight.

To help residents navigate the weather conditions ahead, the Fort Drum Safety Office hosts a Winter Driving Course on select Tuesdays, from 2 to 3 p.m. and 5 to 6 p.m. in Bldg. 4884 on Jones Street. The Snowblower Operation course is held on alternating schedules from 3:15 to 4 p.m. and 6:15 to 7 p.m.

Class size is limited to 12 participants per session, and reservations can be made by calling 315-772-0310. Class dates can be found on the My Army Post App (MAPA). The Safety Office also offers a “train the trainer” class by unit request.

Ewers charged leaders to identify new Soldiers in their units who’ve never experienced winter weather before.

“Let’s not make this a resource that’s out there, and hope (Soldiers) get to it,” Ewers said. “Let’s identify who needs it, and then guide them to that resource.”

The Fort Drum Directorate of Family and Morale, Welfare and Recreation announced an extensive slate of holiday community events and recreation opportunities to include:

Bowl for Turkeys: Pine Plains Bowling Center will host Turkey Giveaway drawings from 5 to 7 p.m. Nov. 5-7, Nov. 12-14, and Nov. 19-21. Bowlers who roll a strike can also earn a free 7-inch one-topping pizza (limit one per person).

Cozy Igloo Nights at The Peak: Private 75-minute reservations for up to six people inside heated, illuminated outdoor igloos opening Nov. 9. Packages include shareables, dessert samplers, and beverages. For reservations, call 315-772-6222.

“Home for the Holidays” Thanksgiving Dinner: A free community Thanksgiving meal will be served from 1 to 4 p.m. on Thanksgiving Day, Nov. 26, inside The Peak. Active-duty service members, Department of the Army civilians, retirees, veterans, and their families are welcome.

Annual Tree Lighting and Holiday Celebration: Ring in the winter season with the holiday tree lighting and family activities at 6 p.m. Dec. 4 at The Peak.

The U.S. Army Medical Department Activity-Fort Drum reminded beneficiaries that TRICARE Open Season is underway. Beneficiaries enrolled in TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select can make plan changes for the upcoming calendar year, with changes taking effect Jan. 1.

For assistance or regional enrollment support, contact Humana Military (East Region) at (800) 444-5445 or visit www.tricare.mil/east.

Beneficiaries can also access appointment scheduling, secure messaging, and lab results via the MHS GENESIS Patient Portal, or use remote check-in for the Guthrie Clinic pharmacy by texting “Get in line” to 833-564-4369.

What Fort Drum families need to know

Army Community Service announced that the Family Advocacy Program (FAP), Exceptional Family Member Program (EFMP), and New Parent Support Program (NPSP) are transitioning offices to the main ACS facility, Bldg. 11042 on Mount Belvedere Boulevard throughout November.

The next Parent Advisory Board meeting is scheduled from 11:45 a.m. to 12:45 p.m. Jan. 21 at the Youth Center, Bldg. 10788 on Chapel Drive. Attending parents earn participation points toward CYS childcare discounts.

The Youth Center on Chapel Drive offers free enrollment for students in grades 6–12, interested in STEM Club sessions (Nov. 5, 12, and 19 from 4:30 to 5:30 p.m.) and All-Star Indoor Softball (Nov. 6, 13, and 20 from 4 to 5 p.m.).

Free enrollment is available for children, between 6 and 18, to participate in the Presidential Fitness Test on Dec. 4 at the CYS Youth Sports and Fitness Center, Bldg. 10790 Chapel Drive. For more information, call 315-772-6718 or visit the center.

Transitioning families moving in or out of Fort Drum can borrow kitchen essentials, cookware, dishes, small appliances, and folding tables and chairs at the Army Community Service’s Lending Closet, Bldg. 11042 on Mount Belvedere Blvd.

And in other news

The Transition Assistance Program will host a Career Fair from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. Nov. 5 at The Peak, connecting transitioning service members and spouses with more than 90 local and national employers.

Soldiers and family members can register through the Transition Assistance Program to attend a new “Getting Started in Cybersecurity and AI for Transitioning Veterans” class, in person or virtual. Class dates are 9 a.m. Nov. 19 and Dec. 17 in Clark Hall. To register, call 315-772-3434.

The American Red Cross is hosting a blood drive from 9:30 a.m. to 2:30 p.m. Nov. 13 at Guthrie Army Health Clinic; from noon to 5 p.m. Dec. 1 at the Fort Drum USO; and from noon to 5 p.m. Dec. 7 at the BOSS Center. Appointments can be made at www.redcrossblood.org. Units can sponsor a command blood drive by calling 315-317-9379 or 315-518-9982, or email katie.loffert@redcross.org.

title: TRICARE Open Season Nov. 9-Dec. 8, 2026: What to Know - Columbus Times
description:
People enrolled in TRICARE Reserve Select, TRICARE Retired Reserve and TRICARE Young Adult also cannot make changes through open season.
That deadline is later than the Dec. 8 closing date for TRICARE health plan open season.
TRICARE health plan open season ends Dec. 8, while FEDVIP open season runs through Dec. 14.
Its official open season website provides an Open Season Roadmap PDF, a Plan Finder, a Compare Plans tool and a Health Plan Costs page.
Health plan open season runs from Nov. 9 through Dec. 8, 2026, while the separate FEDVIP dental and vision period continues through Dec. 14.
text:
Source: TRICARE Official Open Season Information; milConnect; BENEFEDS

Category: Military / Health

COLUMBUS, Ga. - TRICARE open season begins Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, giving eligible beneficiaries until Dec. 8 to enroll in or change certain military health plans for coverage beginning Jan. 1, 2027. According to TRICARE's official open season guidance, the annual enrollment period applies to people who have or are eligible for TRICARE Prime options or TRICARE Select, while several other categories of beneficiaries cannot make changes through this process. Those who are satisfied with their existing coverage generally do not need to take action because their enrollment continues automatically.

Buy Maps

The enrollment period lasts 30 calendar days, beginning Nov. 9 and ending Dec. 8. TRICARE says eligible beneficiaries can remain in their current plans, enroll if they are eligible but not enrolled, switch between qualifying plans, or change between individual and family enrollment. Separate federal dental and vision enrollment dates also begin Nov. 9, with a later Dec. 14 deadline.

1. When does TRICARE open season begin and end?

According to the official TRICARE open season website, enrollment for the 2027 coverage year begins Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, and continues through Tuesday, Dec. 8, 2026. The enrollment window includes 22 calendar days in November, from Nov. 9 through Nov. 30, and eight days in December. That makes the total enrollment period 30 calendar days.

Any qualifying enrollment or plan changes completed during the open season take effect Jan. 1, 2027, according to TRICARE. The dates apply to the health plan choices covered by the annual open season process. Separate enrollment rules apply to beneficiaries who are outside the categories eligible to participate.

TRICARE explains that open season provides an opportunity to review existing coverage and make permitted changes. Beneficiaries who intend to keep their current plans do not need to submit new enrollment requests. The program says their coverage will continue automatically unless they make a change.

2. Who is eligible to change TRICARE plans?

TRICARE states that open season is available to people who currently have, or are eligible for, a TRICARE Prime option or TRICARE Select. The eligible Prime options include the US Family Health Plan, also called USFHP, and TRICARE Prime Demo. These are the plan categories identified on the program's official open season page.

Eligible beneficiaries have several options during the enrollment period. They may continue their current plan, enroll in a qualifying plan if they are eligible but not already enrolled, or switch between available qualifying plans. TRICARE also permits eligible beneficiaries to change between individual enrollment and family enrollment.

The program distinguishes between being eligible for a qualifying plan and already being enrolled in one. Someone who meets the eligibility requirements but has not enrolled can use the open season to enroll. Someone already enrolled in a qualifying plan may use the period to make permitted changes or remain in the existing coverage.

Eligibility is determined by the plan categories identified in TRICARE's official guidance. The open season does not apply to every military health coverage arrangement. Beneficiaries should use the program's published eligibility information when determining whether the enrollment window applies to their coverage.

3. Who cannot make changes during TRICARE open season?

TRICARE identifies several groups that cannot participate in the annual open season process. According to the program, active duty service members are excluded from making changes through this enrollment window. The same restriction applies to beneficiaries of TRICARE For Life.

People enrolled in TRICARE Reserve Select, TRICARE Retired Reserve and TRICARE Young Adult also cannot make changes through open season. These exclusions are specifically listed on the official TRICARE website. Their coverage categories are treated differently from the Prime and Select options addressed by the annual enrollment period.

The exclusions matter because the Nov. 9-Dec. 8 dates do not create a general opportunity for every TRICARE beneficiary to switch coverage. The official guidance identifies qualifying plan categories and separately identifies those that do not participate. Beneficiaries in the excluded categories should not interpret the open season announcement as an expansion of their enrollment options.

4. How can beneficiaries enroll or switch plans?

TRICARE provides three methods for eligible beneficiaries to enroll in or change health plans during open season. According to the program, changes can be completed online, by telephone or through a mailed or faxed enrollment form. The appropriate process depends on the enrollment method selected.

The online option uses milConnect. Eligible beneficiaries can access the service at milconnect.dmdc.osd.mil/milconnect/. TRICARE identifies milConnect as the online destination for making qualifying enrollment changes.

Beneficiaries who prefer telephone enrollment may contact their TRICARE regional contractor or designated provider. Another option is to submit an enrollment form by mail or fax to the appropriate regional contractor. All three methods are listed in TRICARE's official open season instructions.

The program identifies the following organizations in its contractor information:

Program or regionListed contractorEast RegionHumana MilitaryWest RegionTriWest Healthcare AllianceOverseasInternational SOSTRICARE For LifeWPS Government ServicesPharmacyExpress Scripts

These are the contractors identified by TRICARE on its official information page. The listing does not itself specify which states are assigned to each region. Beneficiaries can consult the program's enrollment information for the appropriate contact method.

5. What happens if someone does nothing during open season?

According to TRICARE, beneficiaries who are satisfied with their current health plan do not need to take action during open season. Their existing enrollment continues automatically. The program does not require them to submit a new application simply to maintain the same qualifying coverage.

The situation is different for someone who is eligible for a plan but is not enrolled. TRICARE states that a person who remains unenrolled is eligible only for care at a military hospital or clinic, if space is available. That is not the same as being enrolled in a TRICARE Prime or TRICARE Select plan.

The distinction between continuing existing coverage and remaining unenrolled is central to the program's instructions. Someone who already has a qualifying plan can keep it without making a change. Someone who is eligible but has not enrolled can use the annual window to establish qualifying coverage.

TRICARE also explains that opportunities to enroll or change plans outside open season are limited. Outside the annual enrollment period, beneficiaries can make those changes only when they experience a TRICARE Qualifying Life Event. The program uses that term for the circumstances that permit enrollment changes outside the regular window.

6. How do the dental and vision enrollment dates differ?

TRICARE's official open season page identifies a separate enrollment period for dental and vision coverage through the Federal Employees Dental and Vision Insurance Program, commonly called FEDVIP. Federal Benefits Open Season begins Nov. 9, 2026, and continues through Dec. 14, 2026. That deadline is later than the Dec. 8 closing date for TRICARE health plan open season.

Changes made during the FEDVIP enrollment period take effect Jan. 1, 2027, according to TRICARE. The federal dental and vision program is managed by the Office of Personnel Management. BENEFEDS provides information about eligibility and available plans.

TRICARE states that beneficiaries must have TRICARE health plan coverage to qualify for FEDVIP vision coverage. That requirement is identified separately from the general dental and vision enrollment dates. Beneficiaries can check their eligibility and compare plan options at BENEFEDS.gov.

The distinction between the two enrollment periods is important for people reviewing more than one type of coverage. TRICARE health plan open season ends Dec. 8, while FEDVIP open season runs through Dec. 14. Both programs identify Jan. 1, 2027, as the effective date for qualifying coverage changes.

7. What tools are available to compare TRICARE plans?

TRICARE directs beneficiaries to several resources for understanding enrollment options and comparing coverage. Its official open season website provides an Open Season Roadmap PDF, a Plan Finder, a Compare Plans tool and a Health Plan Costs page. These resources are listed together as part of the program's enrollment guidance.

The Plan Finder and Compare Plans tool provide ways to examine available coverage options. The Health Plan Costs page is another resource identified by TRICARE for beneficiaries reviewing their plans. The Open Season Roadmap provides additional information related to the enrollment process.

Beneficiaries can reach these resources from tricare.mil/openseason. The same website explains which plan categories qualify for annual enrollment changes and which beneficiaries are excluded. It also provides information about the methods available for submitting a qualifying enrollment request.

TRICARE's published schedule establishes Dec. 8 as the closing date for qualifying health plan changes during open season. The official resources also distinguish the health enrollment deadline from the separate Dec. 14 FEDVIP deadline.

8. What are the important deadlines for 2027 coverage?

The two enrollment schedules begin on the same day but close on different dates, according to TRICARE. Health plan open season runs from Nov. 9 through Dec. 8, 2026, while the separate FEDVIP dental and vision period continues through Dec. 14. Changes made during either qualifying enrollment period take effect Jan. 1, 2027.

DateEnrollment milestoneNov. 9, 2026TRICARE health plan open season beginsNov. 9, 2026FEDVIP dental and vision open season beginsDec. 8, 2026TRICARE health plan open season endsDec. 14, 2026FEDVIP open season endsJan. 1, 2027Qualifying coverage changes take effect

The dates apply to the enrollment opportunities described in the official program guidance. Beneficiaries keeping existing qualifying TRICARE coverage do not need to make changes for that coverage to continue. Those seeking a permitted switch or new enrollment must use the applicable enrollment process.

TRICARE's official website remains the source for health plan eligibility, coverage comparisons and enrollment instructions. Online health plan changes can be made through milConnect, while FEDVIP eligibility and plan comparisons are available through BENEFEDS. Both enrollment periods begin Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, with their respective deadlines determining when qualifying changes must be completed.

text:
Why It Matters

The Love Lives On Act of 2025 cleared the House Veterans' Affairs disability-assistance subcommittee on March 26, and its Senate companion, S. 410, was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee on March 18. The bill would bar remarriage from ending dependency and indemnity compensation, special pension benefits, or Survivor Benefit Plan annuities for surviving spouses of deceased service members or veterans, and would expand TRICARE eligibility to certain remarried widows and widowers. The Military Officers Association of America (MOAA) lobbied H.R. 1004 in its third-quarter 2026 report, and the House bill is in committee. ​

By the Numbers

MOAA's third-quarter 2026 report discloses $1,070,863 in lobbying spending, up $216,476 from the second quarter of 2026. Spending is up $647,884 from $422,979 in the third quarter of 2025. MOAA lobbies entirely in-house. The filing names 10 lobbyists: Brenden McMahon, René Campos, Jen Goodale, Karen Ruedisueli, Terry Waters, Brian Kelly, April Vogel, Stephanie Rose, Susie Dunham, and Jim O'Brien III.

Broader Context

H.R. 1004 was introduced Feb. 5, 2025, by Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC-9); S. 410 was introduced by Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS). The House bill had 139 cosponsors as of the filing date. The Tragedy Assistance Program for Survivors (TAPS) reported that more than 50 veteran and military organizations support the bill; TAPS president Bonnie Carroll said surviving spouses should not have to choose between finding love again and financial security, citing Department of Veterans Affairs data showing roughly 506,000 dependency and indemnity compensation recipients. At a Feb. 24 bipartisan Veterans Service Organization hearing, House Veterans' Affairs Committee Ranking Member Mark Takano cited the Love Lives On Act as one of his legislative priorities.

The Veterans' Assuring Critical Care Expansions to Support Servicemembers (ACCESS) Act, H.R. 740, was introduced Jan. 28, 2025, by Rep. Mike Bost (R-IL-12). It would codify access standards for the Veterans Community Care Program (VCCP), require the Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) to notify veterans of care eligibility within two business days, and create an online self-service appointment module. House Veterans' Affairs Committee Democrats argued the bill would widen private-provider access without equivalent oversight and could allow veterans to bypass available VA appointments.

The Military Spouse Hiring Act, H.R. 2033, was introduced March 11, 2025, by Rep. Donald S. Beyer, Jr. (D-VA-8) and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee. It would extend the federal Work Opportunity Tax Credit (WOTC) to employers who hire certified spouses of active-duty service members. More than two dozen organizations, including the Wounded Warrior Project and The American Legion, backed the Military Spouse Hiring Act in March 2025.

Competitive Landscape

Disabled American Veterans is among the organizations associated with the Love Lives On Act. Nine organizations are tied to the Veterans' ACCESS Act, including Document Storage Systems Inc., Disabled American Veterans, Wounded Warrior Project Inc., Mission Roll Call, and Zeel Networks Inc.

The Bottom Line

The Love Lives On Act was forwarded from the House Veterans' Affairs disability-assistance subcommittee to the full committee on March 26, 2026, and its Senate companion, S. 410, was ordered reported favorably by the Senate Veterans' Affairs Committee on March 18, 2026. The House bill, H.R. 740, is listed as in committee, and the record does not show later committee or floor action on it or on its Senate companion, S. 275. H.R. 2033 has the status "Introduced," and its latest recorded action is referral to the House Committee on Ways and Means. Across complete quarters in the evidence, MOAA's in-house team shrank by one lobbyist from the prior quarter as spending reached its highest recorded level.

CLARKSVILLE, TN (CLARKSVILLE NOW) – Premier Medical Group, a multi-physician medical practice based in Clarksville, has agreed to pay $2.8 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by improperly billing Medicare and TRICARE for services provided by non-physician practitioners.
Premier has stated the dispute was over a coding issue that it discovered, self-reported and resolved several years ago.
It does not involve any concerns related to the quality of care provided by our team, and no patient or payer was billed for a service that was not provided,” said a statement Premier shared with Clarksville Now on Tuesday.
“Federal health care programs depend on providers following the rules and billing taxpayers accurately,” said U.S. Attorney Braden H. Boucek.
“We opted to settle this matter rather than take on the distraction and expense of a long court process,” the Premier statement said.

CLARKSVILLE, TN (CLARKSVILLE NOW) – Premier Medical Group, a multi-physician medical practice based in Clarksville, has agreed to pay $2.8 million to resolve allegations that it violated the False Claims Act by improperly billing Medicare and TRICARE for services provided by non-physician practitioners.

Premier has stated the dispute was over a coding issue that it discovered, self-reported and resolved several years ago. “This matter is related solely to a coding issue. It does not involve any concerns related to the quality of care provided by our team, and no patient or payer was billed for a service that was not provided,” said a statement Premier shared with Clarksville Now on Tuesday.

The settlement resolves allegations that, from Nov. 1, 2018, through May 31, 2023, Premier submitted claims to Medicare and TRICARE for services performed by non-physician practitioners using physicians’ National Provider Identifier (NPI) numbers, according to a news release from the U.S. Attorney’s Office, Middle District of Tennessee.

“Federal health care programs depend on providers following the rules and billing taxpayers accurately,” said U.S. Attorney Braden H. Boucek. “When providers submit improper claims, they undermine the integrity of programs that millions of Americans, including our service members and veterans, rely on for essential care. Our office will continue working with our law enforcement partners to protect these programs and ensure that taxpayer dollars are spent as intended.”

Under the terms of the settlement agreement, Premier will pay $2.8 million to the United States.

“We opted to settle this matter rather than take on the distraction and expense of a long court process,” the Premier statement said. “Notably, we have not agreed that any wrongdoing has occurred, and we are not being required to enter into a corporate integrity agreement or action plan to remedy any concerns about our conduct or operations.

“We are pleased to have this matter behind us and to be able to focus all of our time and attention on helping our team care for this community each day,” the statement said.

title: Judge peels apart protests against DHA's $1.6B health readiness award
description:

text:
On one hand, a federal judge’s ruling to deny two protests against the Defense Health Agency’s selection of Optum's federal-facing subsidiary for a $1.6 billion health readiness contract is a normal part of the legal process.

But on the other hand: it is not often that a Court of Federal Claims decision compares a protest to how people use lint rollers to remove pet hair and other small fibers from clothing.

Judge Zachary Somers decided to use that illustration in his 35-page ruling against the protests filed by LTS Health Partners and incumbent QTC Medical Services, a subsidiary of Leidos, against the award to OptumServe Health Services. The protests were filed in May and denied on Oct. 9, while the ruling was unsealed on Oct. 28.

Somers’ introduction compared the protesters’ approach to how all capable lawyers can find problems in any government procurement, much like how lint rollers can pick up anything.

The problem for all protesters, including these two, is that it is not enough to merely point out mistakes an agency made in a procurement and count the number of errors. Protesters must instead show the errors have “some significance.”

Enter Somers with a colorful summary of how, in his eyes, LHP and QTC ignored that basic principle:

“Deploying a total of (17) arguments across approximately 150 pages of briefing, plaintiffs have done their best impression of a lint roller, attempting to pick every particle off this procurement.”

DHA awarded the Remote Health Reserve Program-4th Generation Support Services contract to OptumServe Health Services in April over three other proposals, including those from QTC and LTS. The fourth bidder’s identity is redacted from the public version of Somers’ ruling.

There was some disagreement among the key decision makers on who to choose for the contract. QTC was the source selection authority council’s recommended awardee, but the council’s report did spell out dissenting opinions from two members that Optum should win instead.

The source selection authority was not obligated to follow the council recommendations and ratings to the proposals, but he followed most of them.

He did assign QTC a lower past performance confidence rating than the council recommended, from Substantial to Satisfactory. LHP was upgraded from Limited to Neutral, but only on the lack of available information.

Optum was given a “Substantial” rating for past performance, which the court ruling indicates is a major factor in what swung the award. Optum also had the advantage in the Technical/Risk factor over QTC.

But did DHA actually make any mistakes that meet the legal threshold to win a protest in court? Were DHA’s actions, findings and conclusions in fact arbitrary, capricious, an abuse of discretion, or otherwise not in accordance with the law?

Even if the answer to those questions is yes, protesters still have to spell out all of their arguments as to why and essentially help the judge follow along as they make them.

Each and every section of the ruling’s analysis section begins with some variation of “Failed to show,” whether the judge addresses an individual protester or them as a pair.

The court deferred to how DHA evaluated past performance as a matter of precedent, meaning the plaintiffs had to detail their arguments.

“Neither plaintiff even made it to base camp,” Somers wrote.

Somers summarized the protesters’ arguments as “half-developed” and suggested that future litigants read his decision in detail as a reminder that they are much better off with “carefully selecting and fully developing a few key arguments.”

Nowhere in his ruling does Somers appear to have found an error by DHA that prejudiced either LHP or QTC from the award. DHA seems to have done its homework in defending its choice of Optum over the others.

Somers also used the classic kitchen sink imagery to make his point that these protests fell well short of the mark:

“Plaintiffs threw everything they could think of at the court in hopes that something would stick. They came up empty.”

Back to the beginning with a second main takeaway from this one: lint rollers may be valuable tools in life, but are not in the courts and certainly not when trying to get a contract award vacated.

text:
Seeking Mental Health Care With TRICARE or VA Benefits

Category: Uncategorized | Last Updated: November 1, 2026

Written By: MHH

If you’re seeking mental health care with TRICARE or VA benefits, here’s how to check eligibility, understand potential costs and take the first step.

Key Takeaways

TRICARE is health insurance from the Department of Defense. VA health care is a care system run by the Department of Veterans Affairs. Which one you can use for mental health care depends on your military status: Active duty families and retirees typically have TRICARE, veterans who didn’t retire may qualify for VA health care and some people qualify for both. Some VA mental health services, including emergency suicide care and Vet Centers, don’t require VA enrollment at all.

If you’ve served or you love someone who has, getting mental health care can feel like it starts with a paperwork puzzle. Is it TRICARE or the VA? Do you need a referral? Are you even still covered? Those questions stop a lot of people before they ever book a first appointment.

Much of what you’ll read online starts with the plan and skips the question that actually decides your options: your military status. This guide starts there. Find your situation in the table below, see where your coverage most likely comes from and take the first step that fits.

TRICARE vs. VA: Two Different Kinds of Coverage

It helps to know that TRICARE and the VA don’t work the same way, even though people often lump them together as “military insurance.”

TRICARE Is Insurance

It's the Department of Defense health plan, and it pays for care from military hospitals and clinics and from civilian providers in its network. It covers active duty service members, their families, military retirees and some Guard and Reserve members.

VA Health Care Is a Care System

The Department of Veterans Affairs runs its own medical centers, clinics and Vet Centers and, in some cases, pays for community providers. It serves eligible veterans. It isn't insurance, and it generally doesn't cover veterans' family members.

One of the most common misunderstandings is that TRICARE covers veterans in general. Most veterans who separate without retiring aren’t eligible for TRICARE. For them, the VA is usually the main path to mental health care.

Which Coverage Applies to You?

Start with the row that matches your situation. Eligibility rules have exceptions and can change, so treat this as a starting point and confirm the details with TRICARE or the VA.

Your situationWhere mental health coverage usually comes fromYour first stepActive duty service memberTRICARE, at no cost to youGo to the mental health clinic at your military hospital or clinic, or talk with your primary care manager about a referral for civilian care.Spouse or child of an active duty memberTRICARE Prime or TRICARE SelectLook for a network mental health provider through TRICARE’s provider directory or your regional contractor.National Guard or Reserve memberActive duty TRICARE coverage while on qualifying orders; otherwise, TRICARE Reserve Select if you’ve purchased itCheck your current coverage in milConnect. You may also be eligible for Vet Center services.Leaving the military without retiringUp to 180 days of transitional TRICARE coverage if you qualify, then VA health care if you’re eligibleConfirm your transitional coverage in milConnect before you separate, and apply for VA health care early.Military retiree, including medical retirementTRICARE, plus VA health care if you qualifyConsider enrolling in both. Use the VA for service-connected conditions and TRICARE for other care.Veteran who separated without retiringVA health care (usually not TRICARE)Apply for VA health care online or by phone, or visit a Vet Center, which doesn’t require enrollment.Spouse or child of a veteran with a permanent and total service-connected disability, or who died from a service-connected conditionCHAMPVA, if you don’t qualify for TRICAREApply for CHAMPVA through the VA.

If you’re a military spouse or family member, our guide to support for military families covers resources built for you.

Getting Mental Health Care With TRICARE

TRICARE covers a broad range of mental health services when they’re medically or psychologically necessary, including outpatient therapy, psychiatric care, medication management, intensive outpatient programs, partial hospitalization programs and inpatient care. It also covers treatment for substance use disorders.

The rules that trip people up are referrals and pre-authorization. Some websites still say every TRICARE member needs a referral for therapy, which isn’t accurate. Here’s what TRICARE’s own guidance says.

Before Your First Therapy Appointment

Active duty service members need a referral and pre-authorization for mental health care from a civilian network provider. You don’t need one for outpatient mental health care at a military hospital or clinic.

TRICARE Prime enrollees who aren’t on active duty, such as family members, don’t need a referral for most office-based outpatient therapy with a network provider. Psychoanalysis and outpatient therapy for substance use disorders are exceptions.

TRICARE Select enrollees can see any TRICARE-authorized provider for most outpatient care without a referral. Seeing a non-network provider usually costs more.

Everyone on TRICARE needs pre-authorization for nonemergency inpatient mental health care. Some other services, such as psychoanalysis, also require pre-authorization.

When you call a provider, ask whether they’re in the TRICARE network before you book. Our guide to finding therapy your insurance covers has more questions worth asking.

Getting Mental Health Care Through the VA

VA mental health care covers conditions such as PTSD, depression, anxiety and substance use disorders through VA medical centers, outpatient clinics, telehealth and community Vet Centers. For most ongoing care, the first step is applying for VA health care. After you enroll, the VA assigns you to a priority group based on factors like your service history, disability rating and income, which affects what you pay.

Cost is often lower than people expect. Care for a service-connected condition is free. And through December 29, 2027, enrolled veterans don’t pay co-pays for their first three outpatient mental health or substance use visits each calendar year, whether those visits happen at a VA facility or with a provider in the VA’s community care network.

If the VA can’t see you close to home or soon enough, you may qualify to see a community provider paid for by the VA. That care generally needs VA authorization before your appointment. Our veteran mental health resources page explains how the Community Care Network works.

Care You May Be Able to Get Without VA Enrollment

Some of the most useful VA mental health services don’t require you to be enrolled first. These are worth knowing about if you haven’t applied yet, if your paperwork is still in progress or if you’ve assumed you don’t qualify.

Vet Centers. These community-based centers offer free, confidential readjustment services to eligible veterans, service members and their families, including many Guard and Reserve members. They operate separately from VA medical centers and don’t require VA health care enrollment.

Emergency suicide care under the COMPACT Act. Eligible veterans in an acute suicidal crisis can go to any VA or non-VA emergency room and the VA will provide or pay for that care, including up to 30 days of inpatient or crisis residential care and up to 90 days of outpatient care. Eligibility depends on service history and discharge status, not VA enrollment. In an emergency, call 911 or go to the nearest emergency room first.

Care related to military sexual trauma (MST). The VA provides MST-related mental health care to eligible veterans and former service members, including many with other-than-honorable discharges, even if the experience wasn’t reported at the time.

Mental health care for some former service members with other-than-honorable discharges. The VA makes these decisions case by case, so an other-than-honorable discharge doesn’t automatically rule you out. It’s worth asking.

Using TRICARE and the VA Together

If you’re a military retiree who also qualifies for VA health care, you don’t have to choose one. TRICARE’s guidance is to use the VA for service-connected conditions and TRICARE for everything else. Many retirees enroll in both so they have more options for where and how they get care.

One detail to check: If you have TRICARE For Life, a VA facility isn’t a Medicare provider. Using TRICARE For Life at a VA facility for a non-service-connected condition can leave you with a balance to pay, so ask about costs before your visit. The broader guide to using insurance for mental health treatment can help you compare options.

Frequently Asked Questions

Do Veterans Get TRICARE?

Most don’t. TRICARE generally covers military retirees, including those who retired for medical reasons, along with active duty service members, their families and some Guard and Reserve members. Some people who leave service get up to 180 days of transitional TRICARE coverage. Veterans who separated without retiring usually get mental health care through the VA instead.

Is VA Health Care the Same as Insurance?

No. The VA is a health care system that provides care directly through its own facilities and, when needed, pays for care from approved community providers. That’s why the first step with the VA is usually enrolling, not finding an in-network provider.

Do I Need a Referral to See a Therapist With TRICARE?

It depends on your status and plan. Active duty members need a referral and pre-authorization for civilian network care but not for outpatient care at a military hospital or clinic. Family members on TRICARE Prime generally don’t need a referral for office-based outpatient therapy with a network provider, and TRICARE Select enrollees don’t need one for most outpatient care.

Can I Use TRICARE and the VA at the Same Time?

Yes, if you qualify for both, which is most common for military retirees. The VA handles service-connected conditions and TRICARE covers other care.

Find the Right Starting Point

Military health benefits come with their own language, and it’s easy to put off care while you try to sort out which system applies. You don’t have to have every answer before you reach out. Knowing your status and your first step is enough to get moving.

The Mental Health Hotline can help you understand your options and find mental health resources, whether you’re using TRICARE, the VA or other coverage. We don’t verify eligibility or process TRICARE or VA referrals, but we can help you figure out where to look next. Call 866-903-3787. It’s free, confidential and available 24/7. If you need immediate support, the Veterans Crisis Line is available by calling 988 and pressing 1 or texting 838255.
